item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are now in wait-and-see mode.
Aaron Judge left Wednesday’s game early with right leg tightness. There’s no word yet on whether he’ll have to miss time, and we likely won’t have an answer until Friday at the earliest.
Before then, let’s answer some of your Yankees questions in part one of our mailbag. If you want to ask anything else, there’s still time to do so here.
Note: Questions have been edited for clarity and brevity.
Advertisement
Assuming Trent Grisham is healthy, who starts in center field during the playoffs: him or Spencer Jones? — Ed H.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone told reporters Wednesday that Grisham is running “up to a decent speed” in his comeback from a right hamstring strain. Considering Grisham at normal speed is slow, it’s anyone’s guess what that actually means.
If Grisham is ready to go, it will be interesting to see what Boone decides. There are numerous examples of the Yankees opting for the veteran over an inexperienced player like Jones when the games matter most.
Both players have their warts. Neither Grisham nor Jones is a good defensive center fielder. Jones looked abysmal in center, letting a ground ball go under his glove, dropping a fly ball that hit his glove and nearly trucking Heliot Ramos in right field. Meanwhile, Grisham has trouble getting to balls over his head and in the gaps because he’s slow-footed. There’s likely a higher floor of success, though, for Grisham. Even on the balls Jones has caught, there have been instances where he doesn’t look comfortable reading the play off the bat.
So the main difference will come down to offense.
Before Grisham injured his hamstring, he was not hitting. Calls for Jones to take over were already happening. To Jones’ credit, he has produced at the plate. Even after a dreadful 0-for-6 performance with five strikeouts on Wednesday, Jones has a 113 wRC+. He is always a threat to pop a home run, and that wins ballgames in October.
Grisham has one of the best eyes on the team, rarely strikes out and works at-bats. That matters when the batters behind him would likely be Ben Rice and Judge (depending on his health).
Not that my opinion holds any weight, but I’d stick with Jones in center field. The Yankees can always use Grisham, who’s one of the most clutch hitters on the team, in big spots off the bench.
Advertisement
What will/should the Yankees playoff rotation and bullpen look like? I hate to say it, but Gerrit Cole and Max Fried are not looking like aces these days. The team is winning Will Warren’s and Carlos Rodón’s starts. How are these facts likely to influence Boone’s postseason rotation decisions? … As soon as I say this, Fried pitches a gem. Jinx. — Aaron D.
The American League East race isn’t over yet, but the likeliest outcome is the Yankees will play in a wild-card series against the Boston Red Sox. That means the Yankees will only need three starting pitchers for the first round.
Cam Schlittler should start Game 1. There’s no argument otherwise. Schlittler is one of the very best starting pitchers in the sport. You want your best pitcher going in Game 1 to give yourself the best possible chance of not facing a must-win Game 2.
From there, it’ll be a toss-up between Fried and Cole. Both pitchers have concerns attached to them.
Fried has battled command issues all season, while Cole has allowed plenty of hard contact while not getting much swing-and-miss. I’d lean toward Fried over Cole.
As for the bullpen, the Yankees could have Rodón in case the club needs length. The others likely to be on the roster are Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, John Schreiber, Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Yarbrough and Ryan Weathers, if he’s healthy. I’d leave off Tim Hill, who has struggled mightily this season, Luis Gil and Michael Fulmer.
What is the realistic outlook for second base next year? Jazz Chisholm Jr. hasn’t played up to his talent, which might make him more enticing by bringing down his cost. The infield is already crowded, though, with Ryan McMahon under contract, George Lombard Jr.’s promotion, José Caballero, two first basemen (three if Paul Goldschmidt is still seen as Giancarlo Stanton insurance), and Anthony Volpe’s re-ascension. — Marco F.
What the Yankees decide to do at second base is one of the most fascinating storylines of the offseason.
Advertisement
I agree with you, Marco, that this season has likely cost Chisholm millions. He is nearing the end of his worst offensive season since 2021. He won’t reach the heights he set for himself entering 2026, but he still could reach a 20-40 season. Few players have the talent to post those numbers. Before this year, Chisholm posted back-to-back 4+ fWAR seasons. It would not be wrong for the Yankees or another team to bet on his upside.
Chisholm still offers tremendous defense at second and excellent baserunning. If his bat gets back to being considerably above average, he profiles as one of the best second basemen in the sport. There are valid concerns about his offense, though. His hit tool is considerably below average, and as he ages and loses athleticism, that could be a major problem that he cannot overcome.
The Yankees should consider giving Chisholm a short-term deal, though. He is a better option than Caballero and Volpe, who are better as role players, and few available players are better than what he can provide.
The Yankees should strongly consider playing Caballero or Volpe, who played a few games in the minors there, at third base. McMahon is one of the worst everyday regulars in the big leagues this season, and there’s a higher likelihood of Caballero or Volpe producing at the plate.
Has the Martian played his last game in a Yankees uniform? — oconnell13
It’s a hard question to answer because you can’t predict injuries. You never know if the Yankees will have to reach into the minor leagues for depth.
But it’s not far-fetched to think Jasson Domínguez will never play in another important game for the Yankees again. He cannot be trusted in the field. Every game matters for the Yankees, and there’s always a queasy feeling when the ball is hit his way.
His bat also hasn’t progressed enough to keep giving him chances to prove himself. Jones has leapfrogged him on the depth chart, and the Yankees now have Heliot Ramos on their roster. There may not be space for Domínguez.
Advertisement
What are the Yankees’ pitching plans for the rest of the regular season? Specifically, who’s lining up for the Rays series and will any of them be limited in terms of pitch count? — Nick B.
As of now, the Yankees are lined up to start their best four starters against the Rays next week. Here’s how it looks:
Tuesday: Fried and Rodón are in line to start the games of the doubleheader.
Wednesday: Cole
Thursday: Schlittler
The Rays are also on track to start their best pitchers for that series. They could start Nick Martinez and Drew Rasmussen on Tuesday, Freddy Peralta on Wednesday and Ian Seymour on Thursday. Their rotation is dependent on what they decide to do for their weekend series against the Boston Red Sox. But if they wanted, all of these pitchers could factor into their pitching plans next week.
Any chance the Yanks consider Ben Rice as the backup catcher on the postseason roster to free up an extra bench spot for someone more versatile (and better than) Ali Sánchez/J.C. Escarra? — Matthew L.
The odds of this happening are close to zero.
Earlier in the season, Rice kept catching behind the scenes. Before games, he’d catch bullpens and do on-field drills with director of catching Tanner Swanson. Rice hasn’t done any of that in months.
If anything, Rice would only be used in an emergency situation. Believe it or not, the organization believes in Sánchez. That’s why they didn’t promote Mitch Garver. Sánchez is out of minor league options, so they’d have to designate him for assignment and risk him getting claimed off waivers. They value the consistency he provides to their pitchers, and they think he’s a better defender than the metrics show.

item.title: [NBC Sports] Anthony Volpe delivers clutch double
item.dc:creator: Anthony Volpe
item.description:
Anthony Volpe went 2-for-5 with a double, two RBI, and a steal as the Yankees fell to the Twins 5-4 in 13 innings on Wednesday.
Volpe came up in the top of the ninth with two on, two out, and the Yankees trailing by two. He delivered a two-run double off Minnesota closer Yoendrys Gómez, continuing his hot hitting since being recalled from Triple-A. Volpe has now started six of the team’s past seven games at second base with Jazz Chisholm Jr. on the IL.

item.content:encoded:
On Tuesday night, the New York Yankees played the second game of their series with the Minnesota Twins at Target Field.
They won by a score of 8-1.
The Yankees will now look to go for the sweep on Wednesday afternoon.
UPDATE: The Yankees lost 5-4 on Wednesday.
Chisholm Jr. Sends Out Heartfelt Post
The Yankees continue to play without one of their best players, as Jazz Chisholm Jr. has been out since September 8.
MLB.com wrote (on September 10): “Went on the IL on Sept. 10 and will have no baseball activities for 7-10 days. Said Sept. 10 he expects to be activated for homestand that begins Sept. 22.”
Ahead of Tuesday’s game, Chisholm Jr. (and Jazz Chisholm Foundation) made a joint post to Instagram.
They wrote: “Honored to spend time on the trading floor with Cantor Fitzgerald for its annual Charity Day, marking 25 years since September 11. A meaningful day remembering those we lost while coming together to raise funds for hundreds of charities and continue a legacy of giving back. Thank you to Cantor Fitzgerald and the @cfrelieffund for letting us be part of this special day. ❤️”
Here’s what people were saying in the comments:
Cantor Fitzgerald Relief Fund: “We were so happy to have Jazz and the Jazz Chisholm Foundation return for this year’s Charity Day! Thank you for helping us turn a solemn day of remembrance into a powerful day of giving❤️”
@pr11nc33_: “Will you play in the World Series?”
@anttheplug: “You’re gonna be the ALCS MVP and get paid my brother. Stay positive and work through it we need you big dawg dog💪🏽”
@sead_ka: “Bro please resign with NY 🙏”
Yankees Right Now
The Yankees are the second-place team in the American League East with an 88-63 record in 151 games.
After the Twins, they will start a series against the Arizona Diamondbacks that starts on Friday night in Phoenix.
Currently, the Yankees are 3.5 games back of the Tampa Bay Rays.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are facing a big decision with infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr. this offseason. He's set to hit the open market, and finding someone as talented as him might be hard to come by.
But he had a down 2026 season, and it would not be a huge surprise if the Yankees decided to pick someone else to upgrade their infield. However, Chisholm might have the ball in his court this offseason if the Yankees extend the qualifying offer.
Bleacher Report's Tim Kelly is urging Chisholm to accept that $21.05 million qualifying offer if the Yankees extend it, as his down 2026 season might lead to a weaker free agent market, and Chisholm could look to prove he's worth more for next offseason.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. urged to accept qualifying offer from Yankees if they extend it
"If the Yankees extend a qualifying offer to Chisholm - which was worth $21.05 million last offseason - the 28-year-old would probably be wise to take it and hope for a rebound season in 2027," Kelly writes.
While Chisholm could hit the open market after the 2026 season and seek out a long-term deal, his mediocre at-best 2026 season might result in a weaker free agent market.
He's currently on the injured list and is making $10.16 million this season. If he were playing at his best ability, he'd easily double that contract value on a long-term deal.
But instead, the infielder has 1.4 bWAR this season across 134 games with a .715 OPS and 98 OPS+, the lowest and second-lowest marks of his MLB career, respectively.
Seeking out a large multi-year deal worth north of $20 million per-year after such a season isn't very likely. While he's bound to receive interest, it's not likely to be the kind of deal he really wants to accept.
Instead, if he accepts the one-year qualifying offer from the Yankees, which would be somewhere around $21.05 million, he could wind up landing a massive new deal during the 2027-2028 free agency if he has a strong 2027 season.
It's a risk for Chisholm, but if he's willing to bet on himself putting up more similar numbers to his 2025 season with a 122 OPS+, then Chisholm should listen to Kelly's urging and take the qualifying offer if the Yankees extend it.

item.content:encoded:
All Micah Franklin ever did was hit. In the minor leagues, MLB, KBO, and NPB, it didn’t matter. After a career of waiting for his shot, he translated all the base hits he kept in storage into Cody Bellinger’s bat.
When Franklin learned on the fly through the professional ranks, teaching hitting looked very different.
“It was a little different back in the olden days, as we call them,” Franklin said with a chuckle. “We didn’t have a hitting coach.”
Franklin and his teammates depended on the “hitting coordinator,” who came around once or twice a season. Traditionally considered a grind, minor league baseball has since seen legitimate facilities and pay structure upgrades. In contrast, during Franklin’s time, they made the most of what they had.
“I didn’t have a cage until my second year in Triple-A. By then, I think I was in the fifth year of my minor league career,” he said. “We had tees, and then sometimes we would soft toss to each other against the chain-link fence. You know, this was minor league ball. So you had to figure out what you were doing in a game.”
Still, the challenging environment was no match for Franklin’s blistering bat. Across a substantial sample of 1,141 minor league games, he posted an .866 OPS, mashed 200 home runs, and had more than 1,000 hits.
His success carried overseas when he played in Korea and Japan, posting an OPS of .887 across four seasons.
It’s no surprise Franklin was such a consistent offensive threat because one of his mentors was the always docile, yet superlative Willie McGee.
“I met Willie McGee at 19. In the offseason, I got a lot of work in with him; we would go 500 swings a day. No coaching, really, just talking about different things and how to hit the ball,” Franklin said.
“It was more like, ‘Hey, stay inside the ball. Let’s go the other way.’ You’d start left-handed. The first 25 swings the other way, then 25 swings up the middle, left-center; 25 swings; 25 line drives up the middle; 25 line drives right-center. Then you go right-handed and reverse it. Now, if you hit a pop-up or roll over, you don’t count that. Your concentration is on the task, so you’re hitting line drives. You’re not trying to hit the ball as hard and far as you can. You’re trying to have bat control and body control that way.”
Franklin implements the skills he acquired as a successful professional player in his post-pro career as a hitting coach.
As a coach, Franklin emphasizes a program he’s titled “7 to 22.” The approach is simple: If you attack the ball between 7 and 22 degrees, it creates a bat path that promotes consistency and builds a steady foundation for success.
Some see Franklin’s philosophy and assume he’s created a cookie-cutter mentality for all hitters. In reality, it’s anything but.
“I do not teach hitting one way,” Franklin said. “A lot of people will say, ‘Yeah, you do,’ but no. Actually, I don’t.”
Due to his knack for adaptation, Franklin experiments with all kinds of tools and approaches. His experience around the game has led him to a conclusion about all the tech craze surrounding modern baseball.
“I don’t think there are any, in my opinion, advantages of the new technology,” he said. “That’s with me going all in on the new technology, learning, getting educated from body movement to caveats to all this scientific stuff. Because even when I was all in on it and teaching it, I realized that it is hampering the kid. It’s putting a crutch. These kids don’t know how to do anything else now.”
The quick adjustments he learned to make during his own playing days seem to have become a lost art. Kids are struggling to make them, and it’s a trickle-up effect that’s even left some MLB hitters guessing.
“I changed all the time, and within the at-bat, I changed depending on that type of pitcher,” he said. “What got me quicker to the ball or quicker to what I wanted to do in that situation? So I changed my approach, my thinking, so much. In today’s game, kids don’t know how to change enough.”
One of those kids was Cody Bellinger.
Bellinger came up with the Los Angeles Dodgers and had a riveting start to his MLB career.
Over his first three seasons, from 2017 to 2019, he earned a Rookie of the Year, an MVP, two All-Star selections, a Gold Glove, a Silver Slugger, and 17.2 bWAR. It was a start that seemed almost too good to be true.
Then 2020 happened: masks, disease, isolation, and fever dreams. But there was still baseball.
Unfortunately for Bellinger, it wasn’t the same brand he anticipated. His OPS dipped to a then-career-low .789 in the shortened season. Although the Dodgers won a World Series, casting the best kind of shadow over his dormant year, cracks were beginning to show.
2021 solidified the regressive state, as Bellinger’s -1.6 bWAR was among MLB’s worst. Pair that with a sub-.600 OPS, and he had entered career-threatening territory.
This steep and puzzling drop-off left most of MLB questioning the root cause.
Franklin wasn’t confused at all. He knew exactly what to do.
Long before Bellinger was hitting “Belli-bombs” at Chavez Ravine, he was just a kid in the desert, playing on a scout team that Franklin assembled.
“Mike Fedders and I, we put a whole book together for the D-backs because we weren’t drafting local kids. We’re like, ‘What the hell? There are all these local kids here. How come we aren’t drafting them and other teams are?’
“Well, they paid for a scout team for two years. And this scout team was handpicked, so it wasn’t like a traditional scout team. The D-backs paid, and they said, ‘Go and find players.’ So I did.”
That’s where Franklin met Bellinger.
“Cody was there: this long, lanky kid who kept hitting triples. And these fields are big out here in Arizona. On those big fields, all he did was hit one-hoppers or balls off the center field and left-center field walls. He didn’t really pull balls, and that’s what he did. He was amazing. Through minor league ball, he was doing the same thing.”
With Franklin, Bellinger was a lean, doubles machine with a great arm and good defense. Suddenly, after his MLB debut, he didn’t look like that same player.
“He started pulling the ball in his rookie year, went to the major leagues, and then stayed in LA,” Franklin said. “And I’m not gonna say the Dodgers messed him up. Well, I will say they messed him up, but I will also say they made him into an MVP. So you’ve got to give them credit for that, too.”
As Bellinger’s approach evolved toward pulling the baseball, he became yet another pull-happy, homer-hungry slugger who thrived in The Show — an archetype fans are used to in modern baseball.
Franklin knew better.
“When they worked with him, they had him go from hitting the ball the other way to learning how to pull the ball better because he got older, and that’s what naturally happens. Well, guess what? When you stop working on the other stuff and only work on the drills that are helping you pull in the air, you eventually start continuing to pull, continuing to pull, continuing to pull, and guess what? You forget the other stuff, and you don’t even know how to go back to it anymore.”
Bellinger knew what he wanted to do. He’d done it for years. He had the natural juice to hit baseballs very far. But in those deep counts, or contact situations, his new approach took over. He couldn’t find the same swing that once landed him on Franklin’s D-backs scout team.
“Boom! It didn’t work,” Franklin exclaimed.
“So now he’s texting during the season. I think it was the 2020 season, showing me BP on the field, doing all this other stuff. We didn’t have the drills. We didn’t have anything for him to understand because he didn’t have a foundation. He lost his foundation. So at that point, now whoa, oops, he gets non-tendered.”
From MVP to clutter, cast away from the same city he helped to a world championship, Bellinger had hit rock bottom. At a wedding, surrounded by other big leaguers, his career was reborn.
“So at that point, we’re at Jamie Westbrook’s wedding,” Franklin recalled.
Westbrook is another one of Franklin’s pupils, who had a brief stint with the Boston Red Sox in 2024.
“Pat Murphy was there, and Bobby Dalbec. All these guys get DFA’d or non-tendered. It was really interesting. You can imagine. There was a lot of drinking going on since they just got let go. So we’re like, ‘Hey, let’s go hit.’”
Those three words — “Let’s go hit” — may have saved Bellinger’s career. But it literally took baby steps.
“At the start, we didn’t hit. All we did was learn how to step back to the pitcher again, straight, because he couldn’t keep a ball fair. I mean, he opened up so badly that anytime he hit a ball hard, it would either go foul or to the first baseman. It was disastrous, as we know. Everyone saw it. So, we learned how to step. Then we learned how to keep our direction with a swing. Then we learned how to keep our direction while hitting the ball at 50 miles an hour.”
“People don’t understand,” Franklin continued. “They come here, and I tell them to try to hit a ball at 50 mph, but they can’t. High school kids, college kids can’t. I’m like, ‘Dude, how hard is this?’”
Through rigorous trial and error, Franklin and Bellinger developed a process that worked. At times, however, it took some mental manipulation.
“Cody’s such a late starter; it’s unbelievable,” Franklin said. “Well, everyone’s like, ‘All right, Micah, you need to tell him to start earlier!’ Well, that’s like a four-letter word to him. He can’t. We’re like, ‘Don’t you think if he could start earlier, he would?’”
Franklin used drills that positioned Bellinger’s body so he had to start earlier. As the body matures and becomes stronger, more ways exist to compensate for a lack of mechanical intuition. Bellinger is a strong professional athlete, so it was necessary to keep him within a controlled environment while making such finite adjustments.
“We had to figure out different drills where he’s starting earlier and doesn’t even know it, because his body is getting to an autonomous state,” Franklin said. “So we put a foam roller on him, so he just rolls. You know, when you roll your back out or roll your leg out or whatever. So we put that on his foot, and he has to roll earlier. We also used a ball. So it was drills like that, while making sure he maintained his direction; those were huge. Not pulling the ball, just staying up the middle or the other way, just like he did back in high school. We had to find his old self somewhere in his memory.”
Bellinger’s process included two-to-three-hour cage sessions where Franklin said they’d hit the ball only 90 to 110 times. The cycle was swing, talk, adjust, repeat.
After that, Bellinger signed a one-year prove-it deal with the Chicago Cubs ahead of the 2023 season.
He played two great years in Chicago, and then headed for the Bronx, where he’s now in the midst of a newly inked five-year, $162.5 million deal that’ll keep him in pinstripes through 2030 (barring opt-outs).
In the four years since Bellinger was ousted from Hollywood, he’s back on the big screen. His Silver Slugger in 2023 and most recent All-Star selection in 2026 have all but cemented a comeback that’s nothing short of remarkable.
During this recent success, Bellinger has become less of a good power hitter and more of a good hitter with power – like a fellow Yankee legend.
“When I wrote this down way back when I did a scouting report in high school, I said he’s very much more like a Paul O’Neill hitter,” said Franklin. “That’s who he is right now versus the guy that’s an MVP hitting balls way, way out. That’s just not him. Especially at the age he’s at now.”
Bellinger may have started his career as one kind of player, but it wasn’t who he was at his core. Franklin knew, the baseball Gods knew, and even Bellinger himself may have known.
Still, few outfielders impact a game the way Bellinger can, and the stats matured alongside his approach.
This season, Bellinger ranks in the 81st percentile in batting run value and is an elite defender across the board. It took time to re-establish what he once was, but his 9.7 bWAR (and counting) across the past two seasons is profoundly consistent and can only be rivaled by stardom.
Franklin played professional baseball from 1990 through 2004. He traveled to chase his dreams and never found an environment he couldn’t hit in.
Baseball, the game of storytelling, still feels the vibrations of Franklin’s pro career, if not through the might of his own swing, then through the knowledge he’s weaponized to create some of baseball’s best hitters.
Other MLB stars who have put in work in Franklin’s cage include Matt Chapman, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Nationals’ superstar James Wood.
Baseball is a paradoxical game that can’t be understood through one lens, but Franklin’s approach and his athletes’ hard work made a star reborn.
Franklin is still in the cage, day in and day out, shaping the next generation of hitters, and he knows all too well, as does Bellinger, that baseball is a game where you’ll never be perfect.
“In baseball, you can’t put the person in the perfect position; you need to put them in the most efficient position.”

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Los Yankees han resuelto la gran incógnita de septiembre. Vuelven a octubre.
Ahora, el entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, tiene otra decisión que se vuelve cada vez más urgente: ¿quién debería jugar en tercera base cuando empiece la postemporada?
Durante casi toda la temporada, Ryan McMahon parecía la respuesta más obvia. Era el tercera base titular y un defensor de probada eficacia.
Pero la plantilla de Nueva York ha cambiado a su alrededor, lo que da a los Yankees más de una opción para formar el cuadro interior, ahora que cada turno al bate y cada entrada defensiva de la postemporada tienen más importancia.
Los Yankees también cuentan con una opción más rápida y versátil para el cuadro, capaz de cubrir varias posiciones sin obligar a Boone a recurrir a una estructura de platooning demasiado limitada. Una posición que parecía decidida se ha convertido en una auténtica incógnita de cara a la postemporada.
La alineación del martes ha cambiado el debate sobre la tercera base
McMahon estaba en el banquillo de los Yankees el martes. José Caballero fue titular en tercera base una noche después de que su actuación, con dos hits y dos carreras impulsadas, ayudara a Nueva York a asegurarse el título.
Lo más revelador es que Minnesota alineó al lanzador diestro Bailey Ober. McMahon, un bateador zurdo, había vuelto a ser titular en la tercera base en la mayoría de los partidos contra lanzadores diestros tras recuperarse de un esguince de grado 2 en el pulgar izquierdo el 1 de septiembre. Por eso, la titularidad de Caballero fue algo más que una simple decisión de rotación.
No supone un cambio permanente, pero hace que la comparación sea difícil de ignorar.
Hasta el martes, Caballero ha jugado 127 partidos y tiene un promedio de bateo de .235/.292/.376, con 14 jonrones, 49 carreras impulsadas y 32 bases robadas en 429 turnos al bate. McMahon ha jugado 117 partidos y tiene un promedio de bateo de .214/.280/.353, con 10 jonrones, 34 carreras impulsadas y tres bases robadas en 340 turnos al bate.
La comparación de Stathead que se ofrece muestra a Caballero con un WAR de 2,3 frente al 0,2 de McMahon. Caballero también tiene un OPS+ de 85 frente al 75 de McMahon.
La diferencia en ataque no es enorme, pero Caballero lidera todas las categorías estadísticas mencionadas y, además, suma cuatro jonrones más, 15 carreras impulsadas más y 29 bases robadas más. En octubre, esa velocidad extra puede ser importante, incluso cuando no se espera que ninguno de los dos jugadores sea el pilar de la alineación.
Caballero no dejaba de abrirse paso en la alineación
Cuando Caballero volvió de la lista de lesionados en mayo, Boone dijo que tanto él como Anthony Volpe se habían ganado minutos de juego y que los Yankees tendrían que hacer algunos cambios para dárselos.
Boone describió la competencia como una ventaja más que como un problema.
«Es una buena situación», dijo Boone, «porque tenemos dos jugadores que creemos que pueden desempeñar un papel clave para que ganemos los partidos».
Desde entonces, la alineación ha cambiado varias veces. La lesión en el pulgar de Jazz Chisholm Jr. hizo que Caballero pasara a jugar de segunda base la semana pasada. George Lombard Jr. y Volpe se han encargado de la posición de campo corto. Caballero ha seguido jugando dondequiera que Boone lo haya necesitado.
Esa flexibilidad ha dado lugar ahora a una duda mucho mayor de cara a octubre.
McMahon aporta experiencia y un largo historial defensivo. Caballero aporta velocidad, versatilidad defensiva y la capacidad de cubrir la segunda base, el campo corto y la tercera base sin obligar a Boone a limitarse a un papel de platoon.
El caso de Caballero va más allá del guante
El historial defensivo de McMahon hace que esto no sea una simple comparación ofensiva. Baseball-Reference le atribuye 69 «Defensive Runs Saved» (DRS) a lo largo de su carrera en tercera base. Esta temporada, sin embargo, tiene un DRS de -1 en 825 1/3 entradas jugadas en esa posición.
Caballero no tiene el volumen de partidos de McMahon en esa posición, pero su historial defensivo habla por sí solo.
A lo largo de su carrera en las Grandes Ligas en las tres posiciones del cuadro, Caballero ha registrado un DRS de +10 y un Fielding Run Value de +7 en segunda base en 903 entradas, un DRS de +5 y un FRV de +4 en tercera base en 568 1/3 entradas, y un DRS de +17 con un FRV de +10 en el campo corto en 1.763 2/3 entradas.
Por eso su caso es diferente al de un suplente que se pone en racha en el momento adecuado. Los Yankees pueden poner a Caballero en tercera sin renunciar a esa versatilidad defensiva que ya lo hace útil en otras posiciones.
Su juego en las bases aumenta la ventaja. Las 32 bases robadas de Caballero le dan a Boone un arma para los momentos decisivos del partido sin que tenga que reservar a Caballero exclusivamente para entrar como corredor suplente. Si sale de titular, esa velocidad ya está en el campo.
Además, al bate, es mejor que McMahon. Hasta el 15 de septiembre, tiene un promedio de bateo de .235/.292/.376, con 14 jonrones, 49 carreras impulsadas, 32 bases robadas y un OPS de .668. McMahon se queda en un promedio de bateo de .214/.280/.353, con 10 jonrones, 34 carreras impulsadas, tres bases robadas y un OPS de .633. Caballero también tiene un WAR de 2,3, frente al 0,2 de McMahon, lo que aporta a los Yankees más producción ofensiva, velocidad y valor general sin sacrificar la flexibilidad posicional.
Ninguno de los dos ha sido un bateador por encima de la media, pero esa diferencia cuenta ahora que Boone está decidiendo su alineación para octubre. La ventaja de Caballero ya no se basa solo en su versatilidad. Simplemente ha rendido más al bate esta temporada.
Ahora hay una diferencia de 2,1 WAR que se decidirá en octubre
La diferencia más clara en general es la de 2,1 victorias en WAR.
Caballero ha sumado 2,3 WAR en 429 turnos al bate. McMahon ha sumado 0,2 en 340. A Caballero solo le han hecho falta 89 turnos al bate más para crear esa diferencia.
McMahon sigue aportando ventajas reales. Cuenta con un amplio historial defensivo en tercera base, tiene contrato hasta 2027 y puede dar un giro a la situación con un buen final de temporada. Además, hace solo dos semanas que volvió tras la lesión en el pulgar, lo que da a los Yankees motivos para tener en cuenta las dificultades recientes.
Pero los puestos en la postemporada no se otorgan en función del tipo de contrato ni de cómo se te haya utilizado antes. Nueva York ya se ha clasificado, lo que convierte el calendario que queda en una lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, en una prueba de fuego de cara a octubre.
El lunes quedó claro que Caballero puede cambiar el rumbo de un partido con su bate y sus piernas. El martes se vio que Boone está dispuesto a alinearlo directamente en la posición de McMahon, incluso contra un lanzador diestro.
Nada garantiza que esa configuración se mantenga en octubre. Los Yankees aún tienen tiempo para probarla.
Lo que sí ha cambiado es la carga de la prueba. Caballero ya no parece un jugador polivalente al que los Yankees tienen que meter a la fuerza en un partido de postemporada. Parece un jugador capaz de ganarse un puesto en la alineación titular.
Si esto sigue así, puede que sea el papel de McMahon en octubre el que tenga que reducirse.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — Dentro de unas semanas, CC Sabathia, uno de los lanzadores más laureados de su época, verá cómo su número se alza en la valla del exterior del Yankee Stadium, para siempre e intocable. Los Yankees le dieron un título en su primera temporada y una placa para despedir su carrera.
Así que, cuando la leyenda de los Yankees habla de lo que significa para un jugador llevar esa camiseta a rayas, la gente de la organización suele prestarle atención.
Y lo que dijo esta semana no fue precisamente una celebración. Fue una advertencia, expresada sin rodeos, sobre cómo trata la franquicia a sus jóvenes promesas.
El ambiente era informal, una jornada benéfica de golf en Nueva Jersey. El mensaje, en cambio, no lo era. Tocaba un tema sobre el que los aficionados de los Yankees llevan años discutiendo sin que ningún pilar de la franquicia se atreviera a dar su nombre al respecto.
CC Sabathia, cuyo dorsal número 52 se retirará y cuya placa en el Monument Park se inaugurará antes del partido de los Yankees del 26 de septiembre contra los Orioles de Baltimore, dijo que el equipo debe esforzarse más para proteger a sus jugadores jóvenes de la enorme presión que conllevan las expectativas en Nueva York.
En declaraciones a OutKick durante el sexto torneo anual de golf de su fundación PitCCh In, celebrado el lunes en el Alpine Country Club, este lanzador zurdo del Salón de la Fama mencionó a Anthony Volpe y George Lombard Jr. como ejemplos positivos, y a los exjugadores de los Yankees Gary Sánchez y Miguel Andújar como ejemplos a evitar.
El núcleo de su argumento es que a los jugadores del Bronx se les etiqueta antes de que tengan la oportunidad de crecer. Una mala racha se convierte en una etiqueta. La etiqueta se queda pegada. Y una carrera puede definirse por su peor etapa en lugar de por su potencial.
Una crítica dirigida al entorno de los Yankees, no a los jugadores
Sabathia tuvo cuidado de plantear el tema como un fallo de preparación, no como una crítica al talento. Argumentó que los Yankees no pueden eliminar la presión del mercado, pero sí pueden enseñar a los jugadores sin experiencia cómo lidiar con ella.
Contó cómo veía cómo a los jóvenes de los Yankees les encasillaban casi nada más llegar, y destacó una excepción evidente. Para ilustrar su argumento, Sabathia explicó por qué Aaron Judge nunca se vio envuelto en la misma trampa.
«Como es de aquí, quiere hacerlo bien. Y es que he visto a un montón de jugadores jóvenes de los Yankees, ya sea Gary Sánchez, Miguel Andújar o quien sea: te ponen una etiqueta y ya está, lo cual es un rollo, sobre todo para un jugador joven. Creo que el único jugador joven que llegó y lo hizo bien fue Judge, porque bateó 50 jonrones y todo el mundo dejó de meterse con él. Así que es difícil ganarte el respeto de la afición cuando eres tan joven», dijo Sabathia.
A continuación, relacionó esa tendencia directamente con la mala racha defensiva de Lombard y con lo que él considera que es responsabilidad de los Yankees.
«A George Lombard Jr. le acaba de pasar lo mismo. Cometió seis errores seguidos y ya empezaste a oír quejas y todo tipo de comentarios. Así que es difícil crecer aquí como jugador joven y creo que los Yankees tienen que esforzarse más por proteger a estos chicos y ayudarles a entender lo que significa vestir la camiseta a rayas. Habrá altibajos, tienes que hacer caso omiso de los rumores y salir a jugar al béisbol todos los días», dijo Sabathia.
Volpe y Lombard exponen el argumento en tiempo real
El momento elegido ilustra perfectamente lo que dice Sabathia. Pocos jugadores han vivido tan de cerca los altibajos de Nueva York esta temporada como Volpe.
El jugador de 25 años, que en su día fue considerado la apuesta propia de los Yankees para el puesto de shortstop, fue enviado a la Triple A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre tras el partido de los Yankees del 3 de agosto, lo que dejó el camino libre para George Lombard Jr., la mayor promesa del club. Volpe no volvió hasta más de un mes después, y solo cuando Jazz Chisholm Jr. se lesionó el pulgar.
Cuando por fin volvió el 10 de septiembre, el novato de los Yankees respondió de la mejor manera posible. Jugando en una nueva posición, la segunda base, Volpe conectó un grand slam e impulsó cinco carreras —su mejor marca personal— en la victoria por 10-3 sobre Colorado, y luego salió a saludar al público mientras los aficionados coreaban su nombre. Acabó con 3 de 4 y una base robada. Fue su segundo grand slam de su carrera en la temporada regular, que se suma al que bateó en la Serie Mundial de 2024.
El debut de Lombard con los New York Yankees fue todo lo contrario. Este jugador de 21 años conectó un jonrón en su primer hit en las Grandes Ligas durante su debut el 4 de agosto y estuvo a la altura durante dos semanas, cometiendo solo un error en sus primeros 14 partidos.
Entonces empezaron a llover los errores. Lombard cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos a finales de agosto, igualando un récord de la franquicia de los Yankees que solo había logrado antes Chick Fewster en 1921. Según la Elias Sports Bureau, fue la racha más larga de este tipo en las Grandes Ligas desde que Mark Lewis, de Cleveland, cometiera errores en siete partidos seguidos en 1992. El entrenador de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, siguió apoyándole públicamente, pero las quejas que describió Sabathia ya habían empezado.
¿Por qué la advertencia te afecta más ahora?
La crítica de Sabathia llega en un momento clave para la plantilla. Los Yankees dependen cada vez más de jugadores de la cantera, con contratos asequibles, para respaldar a un núcleo de veteranos muy caros. A Lombard, Spencer Jones, Ben Rice y Cam Schlittler se les está pidiendo que asuman una responsabilidad importante cuando aún están en los inicios de sus carreras.
Esto aumenta la presión sobre el sistema de cantera de los Yankees. Ya no se trata solo de formar a jóvenes promesas. Se trata de ayudarles a sobrevivir al «referéndum» diario que supone jugar en el Bronx, donde cada error y cada decisión sobre la alineación se convierte en tema de conversación.
Sabathia dejó claro que sigue confiando en Volpe, aunque reconoció la incómoda verdad de que puede que los mejores años de este jugador de los Yankees no lleguen en Nueva York.
«Si piensas en la perseverancia y la determinación de Volpe, ¿qué otra cosa va a hacer? No va a tirar la toalla», dijo Sabathia. «Esto es lo que ha querido hacer toda su vida. Siempre ha querido jugar al béisbol, y ha pasado por situaciones difíciles. El béisbol es un deporte duro, pero creo que seguro que lo hará mejor, ya sea jugando de segunda base, de campocorto en el Bronx o en cualquier otro sitio».
Concluyó diciendo que la presión en este deporte es única, y puso como ejemplo al novato de Boston, Roman Anthony, para ilustrar su argumento.
«Esto solo pasa aquí. Si piensas en cualquier otro sitio, en ningún otro lugar ocurre algo así. Piensa en lo que está pasando Roman Anthony en Boston. Si eso pasara aquí en Nueva York, sería noticia principal en Sportscenter todos los días», añadió Sabathia. «Es otra historia cuando te pones la camiseta a rayas».
Las cifras que hay detrás de lo que dice Sabathia
Los datos le dan fuerza a su argumento. No se trata simplemente de la queja de un veterano. La posición de shortstop lo dice todo por sí sola.
La temporada pasada, Volpe fue el campocorto de la Liga Americana que más errores cometió, con 19, y eso que jugó los últimos cuatro meses con un desgarro en el labrum del hombro, un detalle que cambia la perspectiva con la que se valoró su defensa en aquel momento. Esta temporada, antes incluso de que ascendieran a Lombard, los campocortos de los Yankees habían sumado entre todos 16 errores, según las cifras citadas por ESPN. Lombard registró entonces un porcentaje de fildeo de 0,925 en sus primeros partidos, con siete errores en sus primeros 20 encuentros.
Esas cifras reflejan exactamente la trampa que describe Sabathia. Un jugador joven de los Yankees hereda un puesto que ya está en el punto de mira, comete un error evidente y se convierte en el centro de todas las miradas. El contexto —una lesión un año, la curva de aprendizaje de un chico de 21 años al siguiente— suele perderse entre tanto revuelo.
La propia trayectoria de Sabathia pone de relieve el contraste que él mismo está señalando. Este icono de los Yankees llegó a las Grandes Ligas con 20 años, en el Cleveland de 2001, y sintió la presión de inmediato, pero ha dicho que llegar a Nueva York en 2009 fue una experiencia totalmente diferente. Respondió a esa presión ayudando a conseguir el 27.º título de la Serie Mundial en su primera temporada, el último campeonato de la franquicia.
Los Yankees no han vuelto a la cima desde entonces, y solo llegaron a una Serie Mundial, en 2024, antes de caer derrotados ante los Dodgers de Los Ángeles. Ahora que el equipo se ha asegurado otra plaza en la postemporada y Volpe intenta recuperar su prestigio mientras Lombard se adapta en su primer mes, la leyenda de la franquicia no tiene que ir muy lejos para defender su postura. La gran incógnita de cara a octubre es si la organización se tomará en serio este argumento.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees' No. 1 prospect, shortstop George Lombard Jr., recently revealed that he had the chance to get some tips from Derek Jeter earlier this year.
Lombard, MLB Pipeline's No. 13 overall prospect for 2026, met up with Jeter in January, according to The Athletic's Brendan Kuty, months before the 21-year-old even made his Triple-A debut, let alone his first game in the Bronx. The young shortstop reportedly asked the Hall of Famer about playing for the Yankees and in the majors, among other topics. But one suggestion from the 14-time All-Star really stuck with the top prospect: "be a stand-up dude."
"Whether that's in the clubhouse or with the media or the fans, whatever it is. Be authentic and be a good person," Lombard said Jeter told him, according to Kuty. "It goes a long way, doing those little things. Whether that's always being upfront and honest or remembering people's names. Just being an overall good human being. It keeps you grounded and keeps you humble and it allows you to keep doing the stuff on the field and producing on the field and helping out the team wherever you can, while keeping all the unnecessary distractions away."
How has George Lombard Jr.'s first stint in the majors gone so far?
Many New York fans will probably be thrilled to hear that Lombard has already been trying to learn from a Yankees legend like Jeter. So far, though, it hasn't been all smooth sailing for the 21-year-old in the majors.
In his first 32 MLB games, Lombard is hitting .218 (24-for-110) with three home runs and 11 RBIs. The highly touted defender also went through an unexpected streak of six straight games with an error in August. While his defense has looked better lately, the 6-foot-2 shortstop has faced some adversity in his first stint in the big leagues.
The Yankees recently recalled Anthony Volpe to play second base for the first time in the majors after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list. So, New York appears to be sticking with Lombard at shortstop for now. And with the Yankees clinching a playoff spot on Monday, the top prospect should get his first taste of October baseball in the Bronx soon.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.

item.content:encoded:
José “Chema” Caballero ha ido perdiendo protagonismo con los Yankees en los últimos partidos, desplazado por el ascenso de Anthony Volpe y la presencia de George Lombard Jr. en el cuadro neoyorquino. El panameño, que había ganado terreno tras la lesión de Jazz Chisholm Jr., ahora vuelve a la banca en dos partidos consecutivos mientras el equipo busca definir su alineación para la postemporada.
Números de la temporada 2026
En lo que va de esta temporada, “Chema” tiene un promedio de .232 con 13 cuadrangulares, 47 impulsadas, 31 bases robadas, .657 de OPS, .290 de OBP y .367 de SLG. Además suma 46 carreras, 89 hits, 13 dobles, 26 bases por bolas y 103 ponches en 59 juegos disputados con Nueva York.
El infielder de 30 años llegó a los Yankees como agente libre después de una temporada sólida con los Seattle Mariners, donde estableció nuevos récords personales en jonrones y carreras impulsadas. Sin embargo, su rendimiento en el Bronx ha sido irregular, con rachas ofensivas que lo han mantenido en la rotación del equipo pero sin consolidarse como titular indiscutible.
Su desempeño ante los Mets
“Chema” en esta serie del Subway ante los Mets entró como corredor emergente donde anotó una carrera en el primer juego. En el segundo no vio acción y en el tercer encuentro se fue en blanco en dos turnos y recibió una base por bolas. La gran novedad para la afición latinoamericana fue su regreso al lineup abridor en el juego dominical, figurando en el orden al bate ocupando la novena casilla y cubriendo el campo corto.
En el primer juego de la serie, Caballero pegó un incogible en la parte alta del décimo episodio y luego cruzó el home plate mediante un hit de Austin Wells en la victoria de los Yankees por 6-3 sobre los Angelinos de Los Ángeles. Con esa actuación, su promedio de bateo subió a .236.
La batalla por la segunda base
La situación se complicó para Caballero cuando los Yankees llamaron a Anthony Volpe desde Triple-A el 9 de septiembre, después de que el joven infielder dominara en las menores con promedio de .333, ocho jonrones y 14 impulsadas en sus últimos 13 juegos. Volpe produjo un regreso impresionante con tres hits, incluyendo un grand slam durante una sexta entrada de seis carreras, en la victoria de 10-3 sobre los Rockies.
Volpe había sido enviado a Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre el 4 de agosto después de batear .240 con un jonrón y 19 impulsadas en 56 juegos como campocorto antes de ser reemplazado por Lombard. Desde su opción a las menores, Volpe conectó .295 con 10 jonrones y 21 impulsadas en 27 juegos, ganándose otra oportunidad en las mayores.
La lesión de Chisholm abre y cierra puertas
Todo cambió cuando Jazz Chisholm Jr. fue colocado en la lista de lesionados por esguince en el pulgar el 10 de septiembre. El panameño José Caballero sustituyó al jugador en la intermedia para el noveno inning, situación que lo apuntaba para recibir mayor cantidad de turnos y titularidad en la posición durante la ausencia de su compañero.
Sin embargo, el manager Aaron Boone dejó abierta la posibilidad de una batalla por la posición. “Caballero ha estado entrando y saliendo del lineup últimamente”, reconoció el estratega. En agosto, el segunda base jugó en cinco series seguidas sin perderse un solo juego del 18 de agosto al 2 de septiembre. Pero en el último mes, ya había sido sacado de la alineación en un par de partidos.
La competencia se intensifica
El último imparable de Chema fue el pasado miércoles 2 de septiembre contra los Angels en la victoria 6-3 de los Yankees, donde se fue de 4-1 con una anotada y jugando en el campo corto. Desde entonces, ha tenido dificultades para mantener la consistencia ofensiva que el equipo necesita en la recta final de la temporada regular.
Con Volpe de regreso y Lombard Jr. consolidado en el campocorto, los Yankees tienen opciones para el cuadro interior de cara a los playoffs. La decisión final dependerá del rendimiento en los últimos juegos de septiembre y de cómo se recupere Chisholm de su lesión en el pulgar.
